newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Neeman, not Sharon, to be Israeli finance chief.
newsitem.headline: Neeman, not Sharon, to be Israeli finance chief.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in a surprise move designed to quell a smouldering cabinet crisis, named former justice minister Yaacov Neeman as Israel's new finance minister on Monday.

Hawkish cabinet minister Ariel Sharon had been tipped as the leading contender for the post, vacant since Netanyahu's party rival Dan Meridor resigned last month in a power struggle with the prime minister over foreign exchange policy.

Analysts said the Neeman appointment could help Netanyahu calm a crisis with Foreign Minister David Levy, who was apprehensive over the burly ex-general Sharon encroaching on his status as coordinator of peace talks with the Palestinians.
Levy had threatened to bolt, and loss of his support would have left Netanyahu with only a tiny majority in parliament.
Investors, mindful of Sharon's reputation for lavish spending in defence of such pet projects as West Bank Jewish settlements, reacted with relief to the Neeman nod.
"Fiscal restraint is the key issue for the whole economy and the capital markets," said Victor Shohet, chief economist at Ofek Securities.

Shares traded on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange notched a record high on Monday, but analysts said the gains were unconnected to the Neeman appointment. However, they added, a Sharon nomination would have sent the bourse skidding.
The prime minister, anxious to shore up support in his splintered Likud party, held talks on Monday with party legislators vying to be named science minister.

The post was vacated by Likud right-winger Benny Begin, son of the late Prime Minister Menachem Begin, in a spat with Netanyahu over Israel's withdrawal from most of the West Bank town of Hebron in January.

Israel Radio initially quoted Sharon as welcoming the choice of Neeman, an attorney and former Treasury director-general. It said the nomination was offered 10 days ago to Neeman, who agreed only after discussing it with Sharon and other figures.
But Israeli army radio later said Sharon, who made no public comment on the appointment, had cancelled an invitation to meet Netanyahu in what it called a possible sign of yet a new crisis.
Sources in Netanyahu's office said the prime minister would consult "from time to time" with Sharon, Levy and Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai on political and military issues.
This was apparently a signal that Sharon's demand to join Netanyahu's select "kitchen cabinet" on key policy issues -- a move opposed by Levy -- had been defused.

"It is good for the state of Israel that Ariel Sharon is not finance minister," economic commentator Sever Plotzker said. "Ariel Sharon symbolised the Israel that closed itself off from the world, that did not integrate itself with it."

Neeman, a prominent attorney and not an economist, is likely to concern himself with microeconomic issues affecting Israel's economy, and leave to the Bank of Israel such macroeconomic spheres as foreign exchange rates, Plotzker said.

Neeman served a brief stint as justice minister, but his indictment last August on charges of obstructing justice and lying under oath forced him to leave the job Netanyahu had given him less than two months earlier.

A court cleared Neeman of the charges in May, prompting speculation he might return to the justice post, filled by Netanyahu loyalist Tzachi Hanegbi in what the prime minister originally termed a temporary appointment.
The prime minister was also set to face three no-confidence motions sponsored by opposition parties.

Motions by the centre-left Labour and dovish Meretz were to attack the government for its "failure to function". A third motion, by the largely Arab Hadash party, criticises the government for the deadlocked peace process and for cuts in social services.
